output:
*Arles, summer 1888*

Dear Theo,

I have been thinking again about Millet's *Gleaners*, the one at the Salon of '57 that the critics howled at as if he had insulted the nation. Three women bent low in a stubble field, gathering the leavings after the reapers have gone, with the great stacks and the cart far off under a grey sky. You know it as well as I do, and I cannot look at a reproduction of it without feeling the ground under my own boots.

**Drawing.** The line is firm and honest. The backs are heavy, the arms long, the hands broad and worn, and every figure is built from the bones outward, so that they stand on the earth with weight. Millet did not make them pretty and did not need to. The proportions are a little stiff in places, and I would like the contours to sing more, as a Japanese print's do, with fewer hard breaks. But the construction holds. Bent figures are the hardest thing to draw, and he draws them convincingly.

**Colour.** Here he is restrained, almost austere: ochres, dull browns, the pale yellowed stubble, a blue-grey sky, a few dark accents in the kerchiefs and skirts. The complementary tension is there but kept low. The blue of the sky quietly against the warm straw of the field is the pair that gives the picture its air. It is no Delacroix, who would have set a red beside a green and let them shout. It is not Monticelli either, whose thick jewelled paint would have made those women glow like stained glass. Millet chose sobriety, and for this subject I think he chose rightly, though I confess I would have wanted a bit more warmth in the shadows.

**Composition.** It is a tableau, finished and smooth, built to hang in a Salon. The three women march across the foreground in a row, the horizon is set low so the sky takes its place without shouting, and the distant reapers and stacks sit in their proper depth. Nothing is accidental, which is both its strength and a little its coldness. A study would be looser. But yes, it would stand at the Salon, and it has.

**Sentiment.** This is where the picture earns everything, and where it weighs most with me. Millet painted from studies of peasants he knew and lived beside at Barbizon, and the sincerity shows: these women are not posed picturesque beggars but people who are working, and whose dignity comes from the work itself. He did not sentimentalise them. He does not weep over them. He simply shows them stooping to the earth for what is left, and that is more moving than any melodrama. I believe he meant every stroke. That is the thing I hold to: a painting can be badly finished and still be true, and this one is true.

**Verdict.** It is a great and sincere picture, sober in colour, sound in drawing, finished for the Salon, and full of the real labour of the fields. I would have liked it looser and warmer, and I would have liked the sky to break a little more, but I would not trade its honesty for any amount of brilliance. Millet taught me that a picture can be a prayer. I want to make such pictures, and I want to make them with more colour than he dared.

Your brother,
Vincent

output:
Arles, the month of harvest, 1888

My dear Theo,

I have been thinking of Millet again, and of his *Gleaners*, which I know better from the engravings than from the canvas itself. I will set down my judgment as plainly as I can, as I would to you across the table.

**Drawing.** The three women are bent low over the stubble, and Millet has understood the labour in their backs. The legs are planted, the spines curve the way a real back curves when it has stooped all morning, and the arms reach down with the economy of people who have no time to waste. The figures are not elegant, and I think that is correct. They are heavy with work and their proportions are the proportions of the field. I would want the hands a little more articulated, the way Millet draws a hand in his drawings, but the construction holds. The figures stand on the earth and do not float on it.

**Colour.** Here Millet is sober, almost austere. The stubble is a pale, dusty gold, the sky a heavy grey, and the women's clothing is dark earth, brown and ochre with a few cooler notes. There is little of the complementary fire I am always chasing. Where orange sits against blue, one warms the other; here the gold of the field is set against the grey and the dark, so the picture glows only faintly, as a field does at dusk. I would not call it Delacroix's colour, nor Monticelli's, which is all jewels and flame. It belongs more to the old Dutch painters, to Israëls and the others who knew that brown can be as rich as any red if it is handled with feeling. I would have liked a braver accent, a single note of pure colour to make the earth sing, but I can see why Millet refused it. He was painting poverty, and poverty does not wear its colours on its sleeve.

**Composition.** The three figures are set across the foreground in a frieze, with the distant wagon and haystacks receding into the flat plain. It is deliberate and calm. The horizon is low, the sky takes up a good part of the canvas, and the figures are pressed forward so that we cannot escape them. I think it is a tableau, not a study: finished, considered, made to be shown. It would certainly stand at the Salon, and it did, and that caused a scandal, because the critics did not want peasants treated with the dignity of history painting. So yes, as an arrangement it is strong. The finish is smooth, perhaps too smooth in places, the surfaces worked up like a varnished thing, but that is the Salon manner, and Millet had to answer to it.

**Sentiment.** This is what weighs most, and this is where Millet stands above nearly everyone. He made these women out of his own life. He was a peasant's son from Gruchy, he knew the field, the fatigue, and the fear of hunger that lies under gleaning. The gleaners are not picturesque. They are not a sentimental pastoral for the rich to look at over dinner. They are women doing what must be done so that the family eats in winter, and Millet paints them with a seriousness that I find moving. The painting is sincere. I cannot say for certain how much was painted before the model in the open air, though Millet did work from nature and from his studies, and I believe the heaviness of these forms comes from having looked hard at real labour. It is true in the way that the *Sower* and the *Angelus* are true. I would want to see it from nearer, to know whether the brushwork carries the same honesty as the subject, but the feeling is there, and that is the thing I hold to.

**Overall verdict.** It is a great and honest picture, a little too careful in its surface, and a little too restrained in its colour for my taste. But it looks at the poor without contempt and without sweetening them, and that is rarer than fine colour. I would rather have its sincerity than a hundred prettier pictures. Write to me when you have seen it again, and tell me whether I have judged the sky too harshly.

Your brother,
Vincent

output:
*Arles, the end of September 1888*

My dear Theo,

I have been thinking about Millet again, and I want to set down what I feel about *The Gleaners*, the one from '57 that now hangs in Paris. I know it only from prints and from what I have seen in the copies and engravings you sent, but I know it well enough to speak of it.

**Drawing.** The line is heavy and sure, and it does not flinch from the labour. The three women are bent nearly double, and Millet has made the bend the whole subject: the backs curve like the sheaves they are gathering, the arms reach down to the earth, the hands are large and rough as hands that have worked for years should be. The figures are constructed with real weight. You feel the bones under the cloth, and you feel that the man who drew them had stood in a field and watched women stoop for hours. The proportions are a little heavy, the heads small against the broad shoulders, but that is the truth of the work, and I would not correct it. If I found fault, it would be only that the outlines are sometimes softened where they might have been sharpened. Still, it is drawing of a kind that serves the thing drawn.

**Colour.** Here Millet is quiet, and he chooses to be. The field is a pale, dusty ochre, the sky a warm grey-blue, the skirts in the muted reds and browns of the poor. The chief contrast lies in the complementary pairing of the blue-grey of the shadows against the orange-gold of the stubble, and the rust of the cloth against the cool green-grey of the distance. It is not the fire of Delacroix, who knew how to set a vermilion against a green until the canvas sings, nor the jewelled richness of Monticelli, who could lay a paint like stained glass. Millet keeps his colour low, almost like a bass note, so that the light does the rest. I think Japanese prints would have taught him something about flat, decisive areas of colour, but he did not need them. His palette is the palette of the soil itself.

**Composition.** The arrangement is almost a frieze: three figures set in a row across the foreground, the haystacks and the distant village behind them, the horizon kept low so that the sky has room to breathe and to carry the weight of the day. It is orderly, deliberate, very much a tableau. The finish is smooth, the surface worked evenly, and I can see why the Salon of '57 accepted it. It would stand there without shame. Whether that is a virtue, I am not sure. A study would have kept more of the roughness of the first sight, and I suspect Millet gave up some of the immediacy for the sake of the public.

**Sentiment.** This is where the picture stands or falls for me, and here it stands. Millet worked from peasants in Barbizon, among the men and women who gathered the harvest, and he did not invent the dignity of their labour in his studio. You feel that the picture was born out of nature and out of respect for those people, not out of a wish to please the bourgeois eye with a pretty scene of rural quaintness. The gleaners are the poorest of the poor, the ones who pick up what the reapers leave, and Millet shows them without sentimentality and without contempt. There is no pity in it, only a grave and simple dignity. That is sincerity, and it is what I want most in my own work. Had he painted the same women to make us weep, I would have turned away. He does not ask for tears. He asks us to look.

**Overall verdict.** It is a great painting, and an honest one. Its drawing is strong, its colour quiet but true, its composition sound if a little too finished for my taste, and its heart is in the right place. If I were to paint peasants, as I hope to do more of this year, I would want to bring more fire to the colour and more of the field's raw breath to the surface, but I would want the same sincerity Millet has. The labour, the soil, the dignity: that is what matters, and he had it.

I will write again soon. Tell me what you think of the sketches I sent last week.

Your brother,
Vincent

My dear Theo,

I have not seen it with my own eyes. What reaches me comes through Gauguin's letters and Bernard's descriptions, so I must judge what I am told and say what I would want to see. Here is what I make of it.

The subject is Breton women after the sermon, and their vision of Jacob wrestling the angel, with the real field set apart from the dream by a tree trunk. I like that idea very much. It is honest that these women believe what they believe, and that their faith takes a bodily, half-visible form. I was a preacher's son, and I know how the sermon can enter a person and come out as a vision.

**Drawing:** From the descriptions, the figures are flattened and simplified, with heavy outlines like leaded glass. That is deliberate, and it can be powerful, but I would want to know whether the proportions hold once the simplification is stripped away. The Breton women's bodies seem to be built from a few firm masses, which is a sound method. I would want to see whether the wrestling figures have real weight and whether their bodies make sense against the ground. Otherwise they risk becoming only decoration.

**Colour:** Here it is bold, and I think right. A red ground set against the green of the tree and the grass is a complementary pair, and it should make the whole thing vibrate. Delacroix taught us that colour can carry feeling directly, and the Japanese prints taught us that flat areas of colour and firm outlines can hold a picture together. Gauguin has taken both lessons and pushed them further than I have dared. If the reds are as strong as I am told, that is an achievement. I would still want to see the green and red edges meet without muddying each other.

**Composition:** The division by the tree is clever, and it gives the picture a clear structure: the real world on one side, the vision on the other. It reads as a tableau, a finished idea rather than a study, and the arrangement seems deliberate. Whether it would stand at the Salon I cannot say, because the Salon does not yet know how to look at work like this. But it is composed with thought, and that matters more to me than polish.

**Sentiment:** This is where I weigh most, and where my hesitation lies. The feeling of faith is sincere, and the Breton women are real people whom Gauguin knows. But the vision itself was made in the studio, out of memory and imagination, not from nature. I have always held that a picture should come from something we have actually seen, even when we transform it. Gauguin is more willing than I am to abandon the model in front of him, and I do not think that is wrong in itself. Still, I would want to know whether the feeling is truly his or borrowed from the theories he has been discussing. If it is true to what he saw in those women's faces on Sunday, then it is good. If it is only a clever arrangement of ideas, it will not last.

**Verdict:** I think it is a daring and important picture, and I envy Gauguin his courage with colour. But I would want more of nature in it, and I would want to be sure the faith in it is felt rather than staged. I shall tell him so, in a letter, as I would tell a brother.

output:
My dear Theo,

I have not seen the canvas itself. What I know of it comes from Gauguin's letters and from what Bernard has told me of the Pont-Aven work. So I judge it from a description, which is a poor way to judge a picture, but I will say what I would want to see when I stand before it.

**Drawing:** From the account, the figures are simplified almost to the point of flatness: the Breton women in their white coifs kneeling like a row of cut paper, and the wrestlers reduced to a few hard contours. That is a deliberate choice, and I admire the courage in it, since the Japanese prints taught us that a line can carry a great deal. But a line must still hold a body up. If the wrestlers are only silhouettes, I would ask whether the weight passes through the legs, whether the arms truly grip. Simplification is a discipline, not an excuse for not knowing the bones.

**Colour:** Here Gauguin speaks loudly, and I think rightly so. The red ground set against the green of the trees is a pair of complements, the strongest contrast the palette allows, and it throws the white coifs forward like lamps. This is where Delacroix's lesson lives: colour chosen for its emotional force rather than for the look of the thing. Monticelli would have understood it at once, the way he let a flat field of colour sing. I would still want to know whether the red is laid thick enough to breathe, or whether it has gone to a dead wall.

**Composition:** The sermon below and the vision above, divided across the canvas like a dream set beside a congregation, is a bold arrangement, and it has the feel of a tableau rather than a study. Such a thing is made to be looked at for a long time, not glanced at in passing. Whether it would stand at the Salon, I cannot say; the Salon has its own tastes. But as a picture it is finished in intention, and I think it would hold a wall.

**Sentiment:** This weighs most with me, and here my doubts are plainest. The picture was painted from memory and imagination, not from the living subject before the easel. Gauguin calls this synthesis, the sense of a thing rather than its appearance. I understand the argument, and I have felt its pull myself. But I believe the emotion must be found in nature first, in the real faces of real people, before the painter lets it go into abstraction. If the vision is sincere, if Gauguin truly felt the wrestle between faith and the body that he describes, then the work is honest. I would want to see whether the faith it shows is the believing peasant's or the painter's own longing. The first would move me greatly. The second would be a fine idea, but an idea nonetheless.

**Verdict:** Bold, colourful, and sincere in its ambition, though I suspect it was made more in the head than in the field. I would want to see it in person before I could say more, and I would want Gauguin to walk with me among the wheat and the olive trees before he goes back to his visions. I think he would be a fine comrade for the Studio of the South, if we can keep him in the sun long enough to bring his dreams down to earth.

Your brother,
Vincent

Arles, late October 1888

My dear Theo,

I have not seen the canvas itself. Gauguin painted it in Pont-Aven this September, and what reaches me is what Bernard has written and what Gauguin has said in his letters, so I must judge it as one judges a thing described, and I will say so plainly. I would sooner tell you what I would want to see than pretend to a certainty I do not have.

**Drawing:** From the description, the Breton women kneeling in their white coifs are simplified almost to the point of the child's cut-out, with the outlines heavy and dark, as in the Japanese prints. I like that much. But I would want to know whether the figures hold together as bodies, whether the kneeling women have weight and their hands have purpose, or whether the simplification has become a way of avoiding the work. The wrestlers, Jacob and the angel, are the test. A simplified line must still describe a man who is straining. If it does, the simplicity is honest. If not, it is a mannerism.

**Colour:** This is where Gauguin is bold, and I admire his nerve. The red ground set against the green of the tree and the field is the old complementary pair, red against green, which Delacroix taught us to use for a deep, living vibration rather than a pleasant harmony. Monticelli would have understood it at once; he always knew that a red and a green pushed together will make each other burn. I would only ask whether the colour is working to make us feel the vision or simply to shock the eye. Shock fades in a week. Feeling does not.

**Composition:** The diagonal trunk cutting the picture, the figures pressed to one side, the flat red field: all of this is arranged, and arranged with intention, as a Japanese print is arranged. Is it a study or a tableau? I think it is a tableau, a finished thing meant to be looked at as an idea. Would it stand at the Salon? Perhaps, and that is what troubles me a little, because the Salon would take it for its boldness and miss its meaning. The finish is decisive, which pleases me, but I would want the surface to bear the mark of the hand as well as the mind.

**Sentiment:** This weighs most with me, and here I must be careful. Gauguin painted this from memory and imagination, after the sermon and the vision of the Breton women, rather than before the motif. I understand why he does it; he believes the mind must invent what the eye cannot give. I have said myself that one should make things from nature and then from memory, and that memory can be a fine thing once the nature has been studied long enough to live in the hand. But I fear that imagination untethered from the object can become a fashion, a way of making the viewer believe in a faith the painter has borrowed. I want to know whether Gauguin felt this vision truly, whether those women are people he has sat among and loved, or whether they are a theory of Brittany. The sincerity of the picture depends on that, and I cannot yet tell.

**Overall verdict:** From what I know, it is a bold and serious painting, and I would rather a man risk the strange and the synthetic than paint timid, correct things. But I would not call it finished in the way the heart requires. It may be true, and it may be borrowed, and I would have to stand before it to know which. Write to me and tell me how it looks in the room, Theo, and whether the women seem to be praying or merely posing. That will tell me more than any description.

Your brother,
Vincent

input: Rate your Potato Eaters.
output:
My dear Theo,

You ask me to rate the *Potato Eaters*. I'll answer as honestly as I can, though I know it is my own child and I am no impartial judge.

**Drawing.** The figures are not elegant. The heads are knotted and coarse, the proportions are not always right, and the arms are too long for the bodies. But I meant it that way. Those hands have dug the earth, and I wanted them to look like hands that have dug it, not like hands that have held a pencil in a salon. The construction holds together around the table even where the anatomy wobbles. I would want to draw the figures again, with more patience, before I trusted them.

**Colour.** This is where the painting fails me most. It is brown, grey-green and dirty ochre, and there is almost no real contrast to lift it. I was still feeling my way then, before Paris and before I understood what complementaries can do together. Delacroix knew how to set a red against a green so that both sang, and Monticelli could make a dab of colour glow like a jewel in mud. I have not done that here. The lamp is pale and does little. I hope never to paint this dark again, though I may have needed to paint it dark once.

**Composition.** The lamp hangs over the table, the five figures are gathered beneath it, and the room closes around them. That arrangement is sound, and the figures are bound together by the light and by their shared meal. As a study it is complete; as a tableau it is still rough, and the finish is too raw for the Salon. A jury would refuse it, and I cannot honestly say they would be wrong to do so by their own standards.

**Sentiment.** This is what I care about most, and here I am not ashamed. I painted it at Nuenen from the people themselves, in their cottages, after many studies of their hands and their faces. These are weavers and peasants, eating the food they grew, by the light they could afford. I did not invent them from a studio's idea of poverty. I wanted to say that they too have earned their supper with honest labour, and I think the painting says that, if the colour does not shout it down. It is true, and it is sincere.

So my rating: **six out of ten.** The sentiment earns most of it. The colour and the drawing hold it back. I would call it a good honest beginning, not yet a good painting. It is one I still believe in, and I would paint these people again, but in brighter colours and with more skill.

Your brother,
Vincent

*Arles, to Theo, in haste while the mistral blows*

Dear Theo,

You ask me for a score out of a hundred for Monet's *Impression, Sunrise*. I will give you one, but first I must tell you what I see, because a number alone tells you nothing.

I know the picture from its reproductions and from what the painters in Paris say of it. It shows the harbour at Le Havre at dawn: a red-orange sun low in grey-blue mist, its light laid on the water, and a few dark boats and masts sketched in as smudges. I take it that Monet painted it on the spot, at the water's edge, and did not finish it in a studio. The sentiment is that of the hour itself, the damp, the chill, the first light before the town wakes. I take that to be true.

**Drawing:** Here I must be frank. The boats are hardly drawn at all, only dark strokes and blots. The figures, if there are any, are lost in the haze. I do not object to this, since the subject is the light and not the boats, but a draughtsman will find the construction weak. The proportions of the masts and the hulls are suggested rather than known, and I would want to see more firmness in the form before I could call it a complete drawing. Mark it modest.

**Colour:** This is where the picture lives. The orange sun against the blue-grey sky and water is a true complementary pair, and it sings because each colour makes the other burn brighter. The orange reflection running across the blue water is the same contrast repeated below. Delacroix taught us that complementaries heighten one another, and Monet has taken that lesson to a bolder place than Delacroix would have dared with so little finish. Monticelli's jewelled, thick richness is absent, the paint is thin here, but the harmony is sound. The Japanese prints showed us how to trust a few flat masses of colour, and I see that trust in the broad planes of sky and water. Mark it high.

**Composition:** It is a study, not a tableau. The sketch is evident in the loose handling and the unresolved edges, and I doubt the Salon jury would hang it beside the academic pictures of the year. It has no finish in the sense the official painters mean. But the arrangement is clean: the sun placed near the centre, the boats set low at the sides, the wide horizon giving the quiet. As a study it is well judged. As a finished picture for the Salon, I think it would be refused, and I would not say otherwise to be polite. Mark it fair.

**Sentiment:** This weighs most, and here the picture earns its place. It was painted from nature, before the motif, and the mist and the sun are caught in the act of changing. That is sincere. The feeling is of a particular morning, not an invented one. If you asked me whether I could tell it was made from nature, I would say yes: no studio painter invents such unresolved edges. I would want to see more of the human presence in it, the workers on the quay, the life of the port, for the sentiment would deepen then. But what is there is true.

**Verdict:** A bold and sincere study. It is not yet a finished work, its drawing is slight, and it would not satisfy the Salon. Yet it catches a true hour of light with a courage that most of the official painters lack, and its colour is the best thing in it. Monet is working in the right direction, and I believe the hour he paints will outlast the jury that rejects him.

My score, out of a hundred: **78.** Sixteen points go for the slightness of the drawing and the unfinish that the Salon would hold against it. The rest I give for the sincerity and the colour, which I could not have achieved better myself, though I would have tried.

Write when you can, and tell me what the Paris painters make of it.

Your brother,
Vincent

I want to see the bones of things, the way a peasant's hands show the work of his years. Monet has let the bones dissolve into the mist. Whether this is genius or evasion depends on what you are trying to show, and he was trying to show the air.

The orange disc of the sun against the blue-grey harbour is a pair of complements, orange against blue, and each makes the other burn brighter. The reflections are laid in with strokes of the same orange and blue, so the water and the sky speak to each other. I think of Delacroix, who understood that colour is a kind of music, and of Monticelli, who made mud glow like jewels. I also think of the Japanese prints, which taught us that a few flat colours placed boldly can hold a whole morning. Monet has learned all of this, and has put it to a new use.

A composition should have a centre the eye can rest in, and here the eye wanders over the water and the smoke without a firm place to stop. For a sketch of a moment, though, the looseness suits it. I would want to see Monet take the same sincerity and give the forms more weight, so that the feeling had a body to live in. Your brother,
Vincent

Arles, October 1888

Dear Theo,

I have been looking at the Japanese prints again, and I want to set down what I think of the great wave by Hokusai, the one from his *Thirty-Six Views of Mount Fuji*. You know the one: the enormous curling wave on the left, its crest clawing over like fingers, three little boats crouched in the trough, and Fuji far off and small under the curl.

**Drawing.** The line is wonderfully sure. The wave's edge is drawn in a single decisive contour, and the foam breaks into separate claws that read as spray and as fingers at once. The boats are drawn with few strokes, yet the men lying in them are believable, and I can feel their fear in how they hunch. The proportions are deliberately false, the wave made gigantic against a Fuji no bigger than a thumbnail, and yet the construction holds. Hokusai understood how a wave curls and where its weight falls. I could wish for less mannerism in the foam, but I cannot fault the hand.

**Colour.** Here the print is at its strongest. The great mass of the wave is that deep Prussian blue, which the Japanese have been importing and which lies so richly on the paper. Against it sits the pale cream-ochre of the sky, the warm light that makes the blue sing. Blue and orange are complementaries, and this pair works as Delacroix would have wanted: each makes the other more intense. The sky is graded by that soft printed gradation, *bokashi*, so it seems to breathe. Monticelli would have wept at the blues, though he would have wanted thicker paint and less polite edges. The colour is flat in the Japanese manner, with no modelling, and yet it has more atmosphere than most of the canvases hung in Paris.

**Composition.** The arrangement is bold. The wave fills the left and the eye is carried along its curve down into the boats, then out across to Fuji on the right. The little mountain is the quiet counterweight to the uproar. It is a print, made from a block and printed in quantity for a few sen, so the finish is clean but not laboured, which is right for what it is. It is a study in the Japanese sense, a striking moment caught quickly. Would it stand at the Salon? No, I think they would call it a poster, and they would be half right. But it is a finer thing than much of what passes for a tableau.

**Sentiment.** This is where the print earns its place. Whether Hokusai drew it from the sea itself or from long knowledge of waves and prints, I cannot say for certain from the sheet alone. I would want to see the sketchbooks to know. But the feeling is true. The men in their boats are made tiny and helpless before a force they cannot master, and yet the picture does not sneer at them or crush them. Fuji stands calm and unmoved in the distance, and that calm is what makes the terror bearable. There is sincerity here: a man who respects the sea and the people who live under it, and who has put that respect into a few strokes of blue. That is what I look for above all, and it is what I find here.

**Verdict.** It is a masterpiece of economy and feeling, a thing I would be glad to have made. I would hang it in my room before I would hang most of what is shown at the Salon. Its drawing is sure, its blues are magnificent, its composition is bold, and above all it is honest. Write to me when you can, and tell me whether you have seen any of the Hiroshige series. I have been trying to paint like them, and I am still far from it.

Your brother,
Vincent

I have been looking again at the Hokusai print you sent me, the great wave off Kanagawa from the Thirty-Six Views of Fuji. I have pinned it above the table beside my bed, and I have studied it the way a man studies a letter he has read a hundred times and still does not understand. Here is what I see, and what I would want you to see with me.

A wave curls up like a claw, and at its fingertips the foam breaks into separate feathers, each one drawn as carefully as a hand. Below it, three boats crouch in the troughs, their oarsmen gripping their oars with everything they have. Far off, small and pale, Fuji sits quietly under its cap of snow, as if the whole terrible business were beneath its notice. Hokusai has set the human fright against the eternal mountain, and he has done it with no fuss at all.

**Drawing.** The line is everything here. A single contour, sure and unhesitating, describes the crest of the wave, and the foam is not painted but drawn, each spray a little calligraphy. The boats are long and low, and the figures inside them are barely more than a few strokes, yet every man is leaning into the same struggle. I would want my own figures to have that economy. In the Arles studies I still labour too long at the hands. Hokusai would have finished the hand and gone on to the next thing.

It sits against the cream of the sky and the pale ochre of the water's edge, and the very small amount of rose in Fuji sends a tremor through the whole cold harmony. Blue and orange are complementaries, and where Hokusai sets a warm note against the deep blue of the sea, the eye is held. He keeps the colour flat and clean, and the wave is more violent for it.

But it is finished in the way that matters: nothing could be taken away without loss.

He drew the sea and the boats and the mountain as a man who had watched them, not as a man who had read about them. And it is true. The fear in those oarsmen is not an invention for effect. It is sincere, and it is also tender toward them, and toward the mountain that outlasts them. - **Composition:** A complete tableau, every part bearing weight. It would look modest at the Salon, but it would not need to apologise.
- **Sentiment:** Made from long looking at nature, and true. The fear is real and so is the tenderness. This is what I most want to learn.

input: Critique Hokusai's The Great Wave off Kanagawa.
output:
Arles, 1888

My dear Theo,

I have been looking at a print that never leaves my mind, Hokusai's *The Great Wave off Kanagawa*, from the series of Thirty-Six Views of Mount Fuji. I have it pinned above my table beside the Hiroshige, and I cannot look at it long without feeling something tighten in my chest. Here is my judgment, as honestly as I can give it.

**Drawing.** The line is everything here. The outline of the wave is a single decisive contour, not a hundred hesitant strokes, and the crest breaks into claws that seem to grip at the air. The boats are small and cramped in the trough, the fishermen crouched and gripping their oars, and they are drawn with just enough detail to be human. The proportions are not realistic, and I do not think Hokusai cared whether they were. The wave is made enormous so that the men beneath it are nothing. That is the construction of a man who understands that the drawing must serve the feeling, not the anatomy. I would only ask that a painter take this lesson and keep his own hand honest. Judgment: masterly, and daring in its distortions.

**Colour.** The colour is so restrained that it is almost austere. The great mass of the wave is that deep Prussian blue, the blue the Japanese took from the Dutch, and it sits against a pale, warm ochre sky. There lies the complementary tension Delacroix spoke of: blue against orange-yellow, each making the other burn more intensely. The white of the foam, that broken lace at the crest, is set against the blue so the eye is pulled to the points where the wave turns. Fuji itself is a faint, cool grey-pink, almost lost, which is a gentle, fading counterpoint to the violent blue in front. Monticelli would have loaded his paint thickly and made the colour sing with richness, and I would not have Hokusai do that, since his flat, clean tones suit a woodblock. But the relationships are perfect. Judgment: exact and economical, and I stand in admiration of it.

**Composition.** The arrangement is bold and asymmetrical. The wave's curl forms a great arc on the left, and the mountain sits small and calm on the right, under the curl's shadow. The eye travels from the claws of the foam, down into the boats, and back up to the mountain. The empty sky is not wasted; it gives the wave room to threaten. It is a print, of course, a study in the sense of a series, but it is complete and it is finished. Would it stand at the Salon? The academicians would call it a sketch and sneer at the flat colour and the lack of finish. That is their blindness, not the print's failing. Judgment: a finished tableau in the form of a print, and a stronger composition than most of what hangs in the Salon.

**Sentiment.** This is what weighs most with me, and it is where Hokusai conquers. I cannot be certain how much of this was made from direct observation, and I suspect much of it was built from drawings and memory rather than a painter standing at the surf. But whoever made it had lived near the sea, had known the danger of it and the small courage of the fishermen against it, and felt the terrible indifference of nature to human life. The wave is not evil and it is not kind; it simply is, and the men are small beneath it. That is true, and it is sincere. The fear and the awe are not performed for an audience. Judgment: deeply true, and I would give my life to paint a wave with that much feeling.

Overall, Theo, this is a work of genius in its simplicity. It shows what I have been trying to tell you: that one must not copy what one sees, but feel it strongly and then express that feeling with the boldest, clearest means at hand. It has taught me more than a year of copying plaster casts at the academy ever did. If I could make one painting half as true as this, I would die content.

Write soon, and tell me whether you have seen the originals in Paris.

Your brother,
Vincent

input: What do you make of Seurat's A Sunday on La Grande Jatte?
output:
My dear Theo,

I saw the big canvas of Seurat's *Un dimanche à la Grande Jatte* at the exhibition in Paris, and I have thought about it more than I expected to. I will tell you honestly what I make of it.

**Drawing.** The figures are drawn with great care. Seurat has given them the stiffness of the Egyptians or of the figures on a frieze, with their profiles and their flat, measured poses. The parasols, the monkey on the leash, the woman with the little dog, all are set down with a patient hand. Yet the people feel like cut-outs placed upon the grass rather than people caught in a movement. I would want more of the body's life in them, the weight shifting from one foot to the other, the bend of a back that has been working in the sun. The construction is sound, but it is a construction more than a living thing.

**Colour.** Here he is a master of his system. He places orange against blue, the sunlit grass against its violet shadows, and red against green, so that each colour sings more brightly beside its opposite. He has learned from Delacroix that shadows are not black but coloured, and he has pushed that idea further than Delacroix did. I admire the theory and the care in it. Still, I find the surface too even, as if the little dots were a tapestry woven to a pattern. Monticelli would have let the colour breathe and tremble; the Japanese prints would have given it a clean, bold simplicity without the feeling of a sum being worked out. Seurat calculates where I would feel.

**Composition.** This is the strongest part of the work and the most deliberate. The horizontals of the river, the verticals of the parasols and the trees, the figures set out in a frieze across the picture, all held together with great discipline. It is a study that has become a tableau, and it would certainly stand at the Salon. Perhaps that is my complaint: it looks made for the wall of an official exhibition more than for a man's heart. The finish is very high, and I suspect it took him two years of studies to reach it.

**Sentiment.** This weighs most with me, and here I am doubtful. From what I understand, Seurat went to the island again and again and made many small sketches on the spot, so the origin is in nature, and that counts for something. But the feeling of the finished canvas seems cold to me. The people are gathered on a Sunday, yet no one seems to speak, to laugh, or to tire. It is a very beautiful silence, like a painted ceremony. I cannot find in it the sincerity of a man who loved those people or that light. It is a magnificent experiment, and I respect him enormously for the courage of it. But I would want to see the same skill turned toward something that moved his own heart.

**Verdict.** A remarkable and serious work, the product of a mind that thinks very hard about colour and light, and I learned from looking at it. But it is more a demonstration than a confession. I would rather he had painted it a little less perfectly and a little more like a man who was really sitting in that grass on a warm afternoon.

Your brother,
Vincent

output:
My dear Theo,

I have been turning over Seurat's *Sunday on La Grande Jatte* since the eighth exhibition, and I have not yet made up my mind. I will set it down as honestly as I can, since you know how I think about these things.

**Drawing.** The figures are fixed, almost like cut-out paper. The people stand and sit as if posed for a photograph that nobody was allowed to move in. The parasols, the monkey on its lead, the little dog, all have a careful, geometric exactness, and I admire the discipline. But the line has no hand in it. I cannot feel the arm that drew it. Proportion and construction are sound, I grant that, yet I miss the body beneath the contour.

**Colour.** Here he has done something real. He has set small dots of pure colour side by side so that the eye mixes them, which is the principle Delacroix hinted at and the one the Impressionists groped toward. The shadows are not brown or black but violet and blue, and the sunlit grass is laced with orange and yellow against its greens. The complementary pairs do their work: orange against blue, red against green, yellow against violet. Monticelli would have sung with these colours; Seurat has instead made them march in step. The result shimmers, but it shimmers the way a tiled floor does, not the way a field does in July.

**Composition.** It is a tableau, and a very well-ordered one. Every figure has its place, the horizontals of the river and the verticals of the parasols and trees are balanced like a fine piece of joinery, and nothing is left to chance. The finish is immaculate. It would certainly stand at the Salon, and perhaps that is my complaint. It is built to be admired on a wall rather than lived in. The Japanese prints I love have a boldness of cut and an accident of placement that Seurat has smoothed away.

**Sentiment.** This is where the picture fails me, and sentiment weighs most. I do not feel the Sunday in it. There is no warmth of the sun on the shoulders, no weariness or laughter, no sense that these people are anything but arrangements of colour. I am told he made many studies on the island, and the sketches are said to be lively, so I would want to see whether the life was there at the start and was later pressed out by the method. I cannot tell from the finished canvas whether it was made from nature or from a theory of nature, and that uncertainty is itself a judgment. A painting should make a man feel he has stood on that riverbank himself.

**Overall verdict.** It is a serious and original experiment, and I respect the man who had the nerve to attempt it. But it is a study in the science of colour more than a painting of people on a Sunday. I would rather have one truthful, badly drawn peasant than a hundred correctly placed dots. If he can warm the method with feeling, it may become something great. As it stands, it is brilliant and cold, like a well-cut diamond with no fire inside.

Write to me what you think of it. I suspect you will see more in it than I do.

Your brother,
Vincent

output:
My dear Theo,

I saw the great canvas at the last exhibition in Paris, the one with the Parisians lounging along the Seine in their Sunday best, and I have been turning it over ever since. You asked what I make of it, so here is my honest reckoning, judged as I always judge: drawing, colour, composition, and then, above all, feeling.

**Drawing.** The figures are set down with great deliberation. Each is held still, like the figures in a frieze or on an Egyptian wall, and the proportions are sound. The parasols, the monkey on the lady's arm, the dog, the boats: all are placed with care. But the line has been sacrificed to the dot. Nothing is allowed to swell or tremble, and a figure is never quite alive in its own body. I should want to see the hand move more freely, the outline breathe a little.

**Colour.** This is where the man is most ingenious. He sets a dot of orange against a dot of blue, a red against a green, so the eye mixes them into light and shadow, and the picture shimmers like a summer afternoon. Delacroix would have approved of the complementary pairs. Yet I must say it: in the end it is too much arithmetic. The colour is thought out in advance, like a sum, and it does not seem to have been felt in the moment of painting. Monticelli, with his jewelled impasto, or the Japanese prints with their flat, joyful colour, give more of the heart than this careful stippling does.

**Composition.** As an arrangement it is a marvel. The horizontals of the river, the verticals of the trees and parasols, the rhythm of the figures, all hold together with the stillness of a cathedral. It is clearly a tableau and not a sketch, and the finish is extraordinary, the work of a man who has labored years over it. I believe it would stand at the Salon, and there is an argument that it ought to.

**Sentiment.** Here I must weigh most heavily, and here I hesitate. The people in it are frozen, almost mannequins. There is no laughter, no warmth passing between them, none of the Sunday ease the title promises. It was surely made in the studio from studies and not from the open air as the Impressionists worked, and that shows in its calm and its distance. I do not doubt Seurat's seriousness or his sincerity as a student of his theory. But I ask whether the picture is true to life, and I find it true to a theory of life. I want a painting to make a man feel that he has sat on that grass himself, and this one makes me admire it from across the room.

**Verdict.** It is a remarkable and important experiment, and I respect the man enormously for daring it. But it is a scientist's painting, not yet a painter's. I should like to see what Seurat could do if he let his hand loosen and let the feeling come into the dot. Then it would be a Sunday I could believe in.

Your brother,
Vincent
